prompt: What keeps fifty machines consistent over time?

choices.text: Typing the same commands on each one the day it is installed
choices.why: They drift from the day after, and nobody types them on the fortieth the same day.

choices.text: A central desired state, compared and reapplied on a schedule
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Cloning every machine from one golden image
choices.why: A clone is identical on day one and drifts like any other.

choices.text: Forbidding administrators from logging in at all
choices.why: Somebody still has to fix things; the question is how changes are kept.

prompt: In this lesson's terms, what is an undeclared difference between two machines?

choices.text: A group variable without a comment beside it
choices.why: A group variable is a declared difference, comment or not.

choices.text: An exception written in the baseline with an expiry date
choices.why: That is the most declared a difference can be.

choices.text: Drift: nobody wrote it down anywhere as a rule
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A workstation that is a different model from the servers
choices.why: Hardware differences are not configuration the baseline declares.

prompt: Why is an hourly reapplication of the baseline a defence against an intruder, not only against mistakes?

choices.text: A setting they relax to stay in is tightened again, and the run logs it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because it blocks every login that happens during the run
choices.why: The run blocks nothing; it puts settings back.

choices.text: Because it reinstalls the operating system each time
choices.why: It only touches what the playbook manages.

choices.text: Because intruders cannot use SSH while Ansible is connected
choices.why: SSH serves many sessions at once.

prompt: A GPO's User Configuration applies to a person when they log on. Where?

choices.text: Only on the computer that is in the same OU as the GPO
choices.why: That is how Computer Configuration is targeted.

choices.text: Only on domain controllers, which refresh every 5 minutes
choices.why: The refresh interval has nothing to do with where users log on.

choices.text: On whichever machine they log on to, desk or reception
choices.why: Right; loopback changes that for shared machines.

choices.text: Nowhere until the user runs gpupdate /force by hand
choices.why: Logon applies it; gpupdate only forces a refresh.

prompt: A domain member refreshes Group Policy every 90 minutes plus a random offset. What is the largest that offset can be, in minutes?
A security filter on the baseline GPO names a group that, by mistake, has no members. What happens?

choices.text: The GPO falls back to Authenticated Users and applies everywhere
choices.why: The filter replaced Authenticated Users; there is no fallback.

choices.text: The baseline silently reaches no machine and no user at all
choices.why: Right. gpresult lists the GPO as denied, which is where to look.

choices.text: The domain controller refuses to save the GPO with an empty group
choices.why: Nothing refuses it, which is the danger.

choices.text: Every computer in the domain shows an error at logon
choices.why: It fails without a symptom.

prompt: The domain GPO locks screens after 15 minutes and the Reception OU's GPO after 5. A computer in Reception: which applies?

choices.text: 5 minutes, because the OU's GPO is processed last
choices.why: Right. The OU comes after the domain.

choices.text: 15 minutes, because the domain is above the OU in the tree
choices.why: Higher in the tree means processed earlier, and earlier loses.

choices.text: Whichever GPO was edited most recently
choices.why: Edit dates play no part in processing order.

choices.text: The stricter one, because Windows always picks the safer value
choices.why: Order decides, not strictness.

prompt: The security team marks the domain baseline's link Enforced, and an OU administrator sets Block inheritance on their OU. Which settings reach that OU?

choices.text: Only the OU's own GPOs, because the block stops everything from above
choices.why: It stops everything except an Enforced link.

choices.text: None at all until the conflict is resolved by hand
choices.why: There is no conflict to resolve: the rule is written down.

choices.text: Those of the team's GPO, and it wins every clash
choices.why: Right. Enforced survives blocking and wins conflicts.

choices.text: Both, with the OU's GPOs winning wherever they disagree
choices.why: Enforced wins over GPOs linked lower.

prompt: Match each Group Policy term with what it does.

pairs.right: makes a link win over everything linked below it
stops GPOs from above applying to an OU
applies user settings by the computer's location
reports what a machine actually applied

prompt: `all.yml` sets ssh_max_auth_tries to 3 and `host_vars/jump.yml` sets it to 2. What does jump get?

choices.text: 3, because all.yml applies to every machine including jump
choices.why: It applies, and a host's own variables beat it.

choices.text: 2, from its own file, which beats every group it is in
choices.why: Right. The host's own file wins.

choices.text: An error, because a variable may be defined only once
choices.why: Several definitions are normal; precedence settles them.

choices.text: Whichever file Ansible happened to read last on that run
choices.why: The order is fixed, not a matter of chance.

prompt: Where do Ansible's variable precedence and Group Policy's processing order point in opposite directions?

choices.text: Ansible lets a named group beat all; Group Policy lets the domain beat an OU
choices.why: In both, the more specific group or OU wins over the broader one.

choices.text: The machine's own settings win in Ansible and lose in Group Policy
choices.why: Right. Local policy is processed first and overwritten.

choices.text: Ansible processes groups alphabetically; Group Policy by creation date
choices.why: Neither works like that.

choices.text: Ansible needs an agent on each machine and Group Policy does not
choices.why: Ansible needs only SSH and Python; and this is not about precedence.

prompt: What did `-f 1` change in the ad-hoc commands of this section?

choices.text: It ran the command as root on each machine
choices.why: That is -b, for become.

choices.text: It limited the command to the first machine in the inventory
choices.why: All three answered; --limit is what narrows the machines.

choices.text: One machine at a time, in inventory order
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It forced the command to fail on the first error
choices.why: Forks set parallelism, not error handling.

prompt: What does `ansible-playbook --check --diff` do to desk's drifted file?

choices.text: Puts the baseline's value back and prints the old one
choices.why: Check mode changes nothing; the file still said 10 afterwards.

choices.text: Nothing to the file; it only prints how far it has moved
choices.why: Right. It turns the tool into an audit.

choices.text: Moves it aside to a backup and writes a fresh copy
choices.why: That would be a change, which check mode does not make.

choices.text: Locks it so that no one can edit it by hand again
choices.why: Nothing in Ansible locks files.

prompt: Somebody installs a telnet server by hand on desk. Does check mode with baseline.yml report it?

choices.text: Yes, as a diff in the SSH task, because telnet replaces SSH
choices.why: Telnet replaces nothing; the SSH file is untouched.

choices.text: No: the playbook manages no package
choices.why: Right. That is what a separate check and an inventory are for.

choices.text: Yes, because check mode lists every change since the last run
choices.why: It compares only what its tasks describe.

choices.text: Only if the telnet server is listening on port 22
choices.why: No task looks at listeners at all.

prompt: What does tattooing mean in Group Policy?

choices.text: An old setting stays after its policy is removed
choices.why: Right. Nothing manages it any more.

choices.text: A GPO that has been marked Enforced at the domain
choices.why: Enforced is a link option, not tattooing.

choices.text: A setting greyed out so the user cannot change it
choices.why: That is how a Policy, as opposed to a Preference, looks.

choices.text: A machine whose name is written into a security filter
choices.why: Security filters name groups; this is something else.

prompt: Why does the timer add `RandomizedDelaySec=5min`?

choices.text: To hide from an intruder when the next run happens
choices.why: It is a load measure, the same as Group Policy's offset.

choices.text: Because systemd refuses a timer that fires exactly on the hour
choices.why: It accepts it; hourly alone is valid.

choices.text: To give an administrator five minutes to cancel a run
choices.why: Nothing waits for anybody.

choices.text: So that many machines do not all start at once
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Every hourly run in the journal shows desk with changed=2. What should happen next?

choices.text: Nothing: the baseline is being enforced as designed
choices.why: Enforced, yes; but a change that keeps returning is a person.

choices.text: Somebody asks who keeps changing it, and why
choices.why: Right. Either a need the baseline lacks, or somebody who should not be there.

choices.text: Run the timer every minute so the change lasts less
choices.why: That shortens the drift and never explains it.

choices.text: Remove desk from the inventory so the noise stops
choices.why: That ends the enforcement, not the problem.

prompt: Which statements about push and pull are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Push needs SSH from the control machine into every machine
choices.why: That is how the timer on admin works.

choices.text: ansible-pull fetches the playbook from a Git repository
choices.why: Each machine applies it to itself.

choices.text: Pull needs the control machine to be up at the hour of the run
choices.why: That is push's weakness, not pull's.

choices.text: Pull suits laptops that are rarely on the office network
choices.why: The same problem Intune answers for Windows.

Put in order how this lesson deals with a hand edit on desk.
items: run the baseline in check mode with --diff
decide whether the change met a real need
let the scheduled run put the value back
